meta.title: Who really said "When in Rome, do as the Romans do"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Saint Ambrose never said it. His real advice (via Augustine, c.390 AD) was about Saturday fasting; the modern proverb is a later anonymous English rendering.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When in Rome, do as the Romans do'?
meta.ogDescription: Ambrose's genuine advice was about fasting, recorded by Augustine c.390 AD. The familiar proverb is a later anonymous English saying, not his words.

answer.label: Not his words — a later proverb built from Ambrose’s advice
answer.authorDates: c. 339 – 397 AD · Bishop of Milan & Doctor of the Church
answer.sourceLine: The idea genuinely traces to Saint Ambrose, but he never said this sentence. His real advice — preserved by Augustine in Letter 54 to Januarius (c. 390 AD) — was specifically about fasting: “When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast.” The snappy “do as the Romans do” wording is a much later anonymous English proverb, not a translation of what Ambrose actually wrote.

source.excerpt: When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast. [Observe] the custom prevailing in whatever Church you come to, if you desire neither to give offense by your conduct, nor to find cause of offense in another’s.
trail: Ambrose’s real advice survives in Augustine’s Letter 54 to Januarius (c. 390 AD): he fasted on Saturday in Rome but not in Milan, and told Augustine to follow each church’s custom.

A rhyming medieval Latin proverb, “Si fueris Romae, Romano vivito more; si fueris alibi, vivito sicut ibi,” is quoted in Jeremy Taylor’s Ductor Dubitantium (1660) and commonly rendered “When in Rome, do as the Romans do” — per Wikiquote.
The English proverb formed gradually: Henry Porter’s 1599 play has a close version, and the modern wording appears by 1777 — per Phrases.org.uk.
Wikipedia notes the saying is only “attributed to” Ambrose and traces it to the Monica–Augustine fasting episode rather than to any line he actually wrote.
source.excerptNote: These are Ambrose’s actual words as Augustine reports them — advice about Saturday fasting, not the generalized proverb it later became.

source.rightsNote: The proverb itself is a centuries-old anonymous English saying, documented in close form by 1599 and in its modern wording by 1777 — long in the public domain. Ambrose’s underlying words survive in J. G. Cunningham’s 1887 translation of Augustine’s Letter 54, also public domain (pre-1931). No identifiable rights holder exists for either.

author.name: Saint Ambrose
author.heading: About Saint Ambrose
author.metaLine: c. 339–397 AD · Bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church
author.bio: Ambrose of Milan was one of the four original Latin Doctors of the Church and the bishop who baptized Augustine of Hippo in 387 AD. His pastoral counsel to Augustine and his mother Monica about conforming to local church custom — recorded in Augustine’s letters — is the seed from which the “when in Rome” proverb is traditionally said to have grown.

misattribution.heading: Why this gets pinned on Saint Ambrose
misattribution.intro: The attribution is half-right in a way that trips people up: the principle really is Ambrose’s, but the famous sentence is not.

items.why: Ambrose never wrote “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.” His documented words, reported by Augustine, were narrowly about fasting: “When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast” (Letter 54). The generalized proverb is a later English construction.
No one “coined” the English line. It accretes over centuries — from a medieval Latin rhyme, through Henry Porter’s 1599 play, to the modern wording recorded by 1777 (Phrases.org.uk).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Ambrose’s pastoral advice to Augustine (c. 384 AD); the proverb is anonymous English folk wisdom that took its current shape more than a millennium later — see Wikiquote’s sourced entry.

context.heading: The fasting dispute behind the proverb
lead: In 384 AD Augustine and his mother Monica moved from Rome to Milan and hit a jarring difference: Rome fasted on Saturdays, Milan did not. Monica was troubled, so Augustine asked Bishop Ambrose what to do.

Ambrose’s reply was a small masterpiece of pragmatism — not a rule about Rome, but a rule about fitting in: keep the Saturday fast in Rome, drop it in Milan, and in any church you visit, follow the local custom to avoid giving or taking offense. That principle of graceful cultural adaptation is what the modern proverb distills.
detailsBody: The same advice is echoed in Augustine’s Letter 36 (to Casulanus), which also discusses the Saturday-fast controversy.
context.pull: Follow the custom of whatever church you come to — Ambrose’s actual counsel, later flattened into “do as the Romans do.”
